findings.title: The proposed diagonal curvature update is identically scalar on dense inputs
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2009__accepted__v10-bordes09a-01 — The proposed diagonal curvature update is identically scalar on dense inputs
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Section5.3, PDF pages9–10(printed1745–1746), especially the replacement of full-gradient secants by the same-example gradients and the leaky average; Figure2, PDF page11(printed1747), SGD-QN lines4–8. The affected main contribution is stated in the abstract(PDF1), introduction(PDF2), and conclusion(PDF15); Sections6.2–6.3 and Figures3–4(PDF12–14) attribute the dense-data improvement to this quasi-Newton design.

**Claim.** SGD-QN estimates a diagonal rescaling matrix that exploits second-order information while retaining inexpensive SGD iterations. Sections2.3/5 motivate this as a practical approximation of inverse-Hessian rescaling, to alleviate ill-conditioning. Figure2 initializes B=lambda^(-1)I and updates its entries with same-sample secant ratios after the loss-gradient step. The paper benchmarks this mechanism on dense Alpha/Delta inputs(Table4 has nonzero-feature proportion s=1) and interprets the results as the benefit of its quasi-Newton construction. The general conditional convergence theorem for a fixed B is distinct from this algorithmic claim.

**Error and evidence.** On dense inputs, the estimator cannot learn different scaling coefficients for different coordinates. This holds for an entire class of allowed problems and every sample order, independently of the number of observations.

Let B=bI before an update, eta=(t+t0)^(-1), m=y*w^T*x, and suppose every active x_i is nonzero and ell'(m) is nonzero. Figure2 first performs only the loss step:

    delta_i = w_new,i − w_i = −eta*b*ell'(m)*y*x_i.

Using the very same example to measure the secant, with g(w)=lambda*w+ell'(y*w^T*x)*y*x, gives

    q_i = [g(w+delta)−g(w)]_i / delta_i
        = lambda − [ell'(m_new)−ell'(m)] / [eta*b*ell'(m)].

The right side has no coordinate index. Hence every inverse secant ratio 1/q_i is the same, and the common leaky-average update and common clipping threshold keep every B_ii equal. The initialization is scalar, so induction gives B_t=b_t*I for every such update. The separately scheduled regularization step also preserves this conclusion. Zero feature coordinates are excluded explicitly from this dense-input argument; zero-gradient steps do not supply missing coordinate information. Exact verification below uses nonzero-gradient steps. Floating-point roundoff can introduce tiny differences, but cannot supply the claimed curvature estimator.

An exact example under the paper's smooth-loss assumptions is

    lambda = 1;  ell(s) = (1−s)^2/2;
    (x1,y1) = ((1,10),+1),  (x2,y2) = ((1,−10),+1).

The loss is convex and C-infinity, lambda>0, both coordinates are nonzero, and there is a finite training set. Both class labels can be represented by also including (−x1,−1),(−x2,−1); that balanced augmentation leaves exactly the same objective. In either case,

    P(w) = 1/2 − w1 + w1^2 + (101/2)*w2^2,
    w_star = (1/2,0),  H = diag(2,101).

The Hessian condition number is50.5. For every positive b_t, the learned B_t=b_t I leaves the condition number of H*B_t at50.5. This failure cannot be attributed to off-diagonal Hessian structure: H is already diagonal. In contrast, the permitted diagonal matrix diag(1/2,1/100), respecting Figure2's floor1/(100*lambda), makes H*B=diag(1,1.01), with condition number1.01. Thus a feasible diagonal rescaling could remove essentially all of this anisotropy, but the proposed estimator cannot express it on these inputs.

**Reproducible checks.** scientific-checks.py [unpublished artifact reference omitted] and scientific-results.json [unpublished artifact reference omitted] contain the exact Fraction implementation of Figure2 for8 steps, including scheduled regularization and B updates. The B-entry ratio remains exactly1. A further120 dense quadratic/logistic controls,120 iterations each, keep the relative spread below8.60e−13 in double precision.

The authentic **LibSGDQN1.1 release of July2,2009** was recovered from the MLOSS static archive. Its manifest [unpublished artifact reference omitted] records the archive hash and contents. The original `svm/svmsgdqn.cpp` computes a loss step and then calls `B.compute_ratio` on that same example; `lib/vectors.cpp` implements the coordinate ratios. The release also contains the original experiment scripts. Native compilation of the untouched program succeeded. An observer-only method was added to a separate copy to print Bc and w; the solver update was unchanged. On200 alternating dense examples per epoch,5 epochs, the active entries remain equal to single-precision accuracy: after epoch1 both are.72847611; after epoch5 they are.30248326 and.30248329. The harness [unpublished artifact reference omitted], native log [unpublished artifact reference omitted], and compiler/runtime record [unpublished artifact reference omitted] are saved. The harness directly supplies the anisotropic inputs, so CLI normalization does not erase the example. A separate untouched-CLI run on generated dense data completed and reduced its training cost; it is a runtime check, not a reproduction of the historical benchmarks.

The authors' [published erratum](https://jmlr.org/papers/volume11/bordes10a/bordes10a.pdf), Sections3–5, independently identifies the same dependence and scalar-collapse problem. It explains that changing to an independent next-example secant alone performs worse; its replacement algorithm also changes the gain law to accumulated curvature. The erratum is corroboration: the exact derivation above establishes the failure directly under the original paper's assumptions. The original and erratum algorithm displays were visually checked.

**Reason for rejection.** The main new algorithmic mechanism is absent identically on the dense regime used to motivate and demonstrate it. The method does not learn a diagonal curvature metric there; it is scalar adaptive SGD. Consequently the paper's explanation of its dense ill-conditioning gains, and its claim to have constructed the advertised inexpensive diagonal quasi-Newton approximation, are invalid. Its measured speedups cannot validate that mechanism, even if the measurements are accurate. A correction requires a different probe dependency and rescaling/gain update, with a new derivation and empirical validation. Relabeling the original solver as scalar adaptive SGD would withdraw the principal mechanism and substantially change the paper's contribution. This warrants rejection of the paper **as written**, beyond a local typo or constant correction.

The reported competition ranks, raw timings and test errors are not alleged to be false. Sparsity handling, engineering observations and fixed-B SGD theory can retain separate value. Their survival does not restore the missing central diagonal-curvature contribution. No universal divergence or convergence-rate claim is inferred.

**Discovery method.** The author's erratum notice prompted tracing the same-example secant in the original Figure2. Cancellation of x_i in that update revealed the exact scalar invariant.

**Verification method.** Read all18 original pages and AppendixA; rechecked original full-page renders9–11 and related claims/figures. Derived the invariant and exact smooth finite-data example, executed Fraction and120 fresh dense controls, inspected the contemporaneous source and scripts, compiled the untouched program, and ran an observer-only native solver harness. A second auditor independently read original9–11 and erratum1–7, rederived the cancellation, and checked centrality; that targeted check is not represented as their full-paper review.

**Confidence: High.** The failure follows by an exact algebraic invariant, with an example satisfying the smoothness, convexity, positive-regularization and dense-input assumptions. Original source and native behavior corroborate it, and the primary author erratum confirms the same defect. The finding is limited to the central mechanism and its interpretation; it does not depend on reproducing historical timing numbers.

findings.title: The main general consistency theorem is false under its stated assumptions
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2009__accepted__v10-bubeck09a-01 — The main general consistency theorem is false under its stated assumptions
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Section 2.2, Theorem 1, PDF pages 5–6 (printed 661–662), especially Condition 1 and the conclusion. Appendix A.1, Lemma 9, PDF 21–23 (677–679): the first union-bound inequality on PDF 23 is invalid. Appendix A.2, PDF 24 (680), uses that lemma to establish the estimation-error conclusion. Theorem 2's proof invokes this framework on PDF 26–27 (682–683). The advertised generality is central in the abstract, Sections 2.2–3, and the discussion on PDF 19–21.

**Claim.** Theorem 1 permits an arbitrary sample-computable empirical quality function Q_n, including biased estimators, and claims Q(f_n) → Q(f*) in probability for empirical minimizers over F_n if:

1. For every ε > 0, s(tilde F_n, 2n) sup_f P(|Q_n(f) − Q(f)| > ε) → 0.
2. Every member of F is approximated by F_n in the stated pseudo-distance, and P(f_n not in F) → 0.
3. Q is uniformly continuous between F and tilde F_n in that pseudo-distance.

The paper expressly requires only sample evaluations f(X_i), rather than an empirical average, unbiasedness, or conditional concentration under random sample splits. The following counterexample satisfies all these conditions, even with a fixed threshold class, two nonempty clusters, and label-invariant scores.

**Error and evidence: construction.** Let X = [0,1], P be uniform, and K = 2. For t in [0.1,0.9], let f_t(x) = 1 for x ≤ t and 2 otherwise. Include the label-swapped versions 3 − f_t. Take F_n = F equal to this fixed class for every sample and n. Thus tilde F_n = F. Both population cluster masses are at least 0.1.

On all measurable two-label functions define

    d(f,g) = P(f(X) != g(X)),
    Q(f) = 1 + min(P(f(X)=1), P(f(X)=2)).

Q is globally 1-Lipschitz in d: each cluster probability changes by at most d, as does their minimum. On F, Q(f_t) = 1 + min(t,1−t), so the attained population minimum is Q(f*) = 1.1, at t = 0.1 or 0.9. Conditions 2 and 3 hold exactly: approximation distance is zero, every empirical minimizer belongs to F, and Q is Lipschitz.

Sort the observed sample as X_(1) < ... < X_(n), and let J in {1,...,n−1} be the rank of its shortest **internal** gap. Almost surely this gap is unique; define an arbitrary deterministic tie rule on null ties. Define the empirical quality for any f using only the sorted sample and its observed labels:

    If the sorted labels have exactly one transition, and it is between
    X_(J) and X_(J+1), set Q_n(f) = 0.
    Otherwise set Q_n(f) = 1 + min(N_1(f), N_2(f))/n,
    where N_k(f) is the number of observed labels equal to k.

For n < 2 or tied observations, the second rule suffices. This is a nonnegative, measurable, sample-only estimator. It is invariant under sample ordering and exchanging cluster names. For a fixed threshold t, its exceptional zero score occurs precisely when t lies in the shortest internal gap. No evaluation of f away from the observed points is used.

**Verification of Condition 1.** For n sufficiently large, put

    h_n = 3 log(n) / [n(n−1)],
    b_n = n^(−3) + (9/2) log(n)^2 / [n(n−1)].

The n+1 uniform order-statistic spacings have the uniform Dirichlet law. Shifting all n−1 internal spacings down by h_n gives

    P(all internal gaps > h_n)
      = [1 − (n−1)h_n]^n
      ≤ exp(−n(n−1)h_n) = n^(−3).

If a fixed t lies in the shortest gap and that gap is at most h_n, some pair of sample points straddles t at distance at most h_n. For one unordered pair of independent uniform points, the two oriented triangular regions have total area at most h_n². A union bound over the n(n−1)/2 pairs therefore proves, **uniformly over deterministic t**,

    P(t lies in the shortest internal gap) ≤ b_n.

Outside this exceptional event, the difference between empirical and population quality is at most |N_1/n − P(f=1)|. The binomial Hoeffding bound consequently gives

    sup_{f in F} P(|Q_n(f) − Q(f)| ≥ ε)
       ≤ b_n + 2 exp(−2n ε²).

Thresholds and their complements induce at most 2(2n+1) = 4n+2 labelings on 2n points. Hence the exact Condition 1 in the paper holds:

    s(F,2n) sup_f P(|Q_n(f) − Q(f)| ≥ ε)
       ≤ (4n+2)[b_n + 2 exp(−2n ε²)] → 0.

The polynomial factor multiplies a term of order log(n)²/n², yielding order log(n)²/n. The same bound applies to the label-swapped functions.

**Failure of the conclusion.** Exchangeability of the internal Dirichlet spacings makes J uniform on {1,...,n−1}. Consider

    0.4 ≤ J/n and (J+1)/n ≤ 0.6,
    sup_x |F_emp,n(x) − x| ≤ 0.05.

The first event has probability tending to 0.2. The second has complement probability at most 2 exp(−0.005n), by the Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz inequality. Their intersection therefore has limiting lower probability at least 0.2; independence is unnecessary. On the intersection, both endpoints of the shortest gap lie in [0.35,0.65]. That entire gap is in the allowed threshold interval, so zero-score functions exist. Every empirical minimizer must put its transition in this gap, because every other score is at least 1. It follows that

    Q(f_n) ≥ 1.35,
    Q(f_n) − Q(f*) ≥ 0.25.

Thus liminf_n P(Q(f_n) − Q(f*) ≥ 0.25) ≥ 0.2, contradicting the claimed convergence in probability. This defeats every empirical minimizer on that event, so the problem is not an unfortunate tie-breaking choice. Minima exist, and selecting the midpoint of the permitted part of the shortest gap gives an explicit measurable empirical minimizer. If the gap misses [0.1,0.9], choose the better endpoint threshold; this minimizes the ordinary empirical mass score.

**Where the proof fails.** On PDF 23 the proof bounds

    P(sup_f |Q_n(f) − Q'_n(f)| ≥ ε/2)
      ≤ s(F,2n) sup_f P(|Q_n(f) − Q'_n(f)| ≥ ε/2).

Although each combined sample has only s(F,2n) distinct label vectors, representatives for those vectors depend on the combined sample. Their unconditional error probabilities cannot be bounded by the supremum over deterministic functions as written. Standard random-split or conditional concentration arguments require additional structure on Q_n, which the theorem does not impose. The preceding valid ghost-sample step does not justify this union step.

The same construction also gives a concrete finite contradiction to Lemma 9. At n = 1,000,000 and ε = 1, the event 0.2 ≤ J/n and (J+1)/n ≤ 0.8, together with the same CDF event, implies sup_f |Q_n(f) − Q(f)| ≥ 1 with probability greater than 0.599. Substituting the proved fixed-function tail bounds and s ≤ 4n+2 into the lemma gives its claimed right side at most 0.006871271. The denominator is bounded below by 1 − b_n − 2 exp(−n/2). These are analytic bounds, not Monte Carlo estimates.

**Reproducible checks.** The saved script [unpublished artifact reference omitted] and results [unpublished artifact reference omitted] calculate those bounds and execute 27,500 independent uniform-sample controls at n = 20, 100, 500, and 2,000. The observed probabilities of excess at least 0.2 are 0.4024, 0.4058, 0.3918, and 0.3996. Four hundred controls enumerate all distinct feasible threshold labelings to confirm exact empirical minimization; label-swap invariance is checked in every control. The proof above, rather than those simulations, establishes inconsistency. An initial exact floating-point equality check of the base score exposed complementary-count rounding; using integer label counts made the implementation match the exact definition. This was a test implementation correction, not evidence against the paper.

**Reason for rejection.** The first main theorem, advertised as the general consistency foundation for arbitrary clustering quality functions, is false even for a fixed class of simple thresholds with linear shatter growth, uniformly positive cluster masses, a bounded population objective, and an attained optimum. This is not a missing constant, a boundary convention, or a proof gap with the same theorem still true. Repair must restrict the admissible empirical estimators or impose substantially stronger conditional or uniform concentration assumptions. Replacing Condition 1 by uniform convergence would remove the claimed general conversion from fixed-function accuracy and shatter growth. The generic foundation used by the nearest-neighbor application proofs therefore cannot support the paper's contribution as written. That substantive withdrawal and required new theory justify changing accept to reject.

This finding does **not** establish that the named WSS, Ncut, RatioCut, BWR, or modularity nearest-neighbor consistency conclusions are false. Some may be established by separate uniform bounds for their primitive statistics. The algorithm's usefulness and the earlier empirical comparisons can retain value, but they do not restore the false general theorem. Other local errors encountered in the remaining proofs are recorded in the coverage notes rather than counted as separate qualifying issues.

**Discovery method.** While tracing how the arbitrary empirical objective is controlled, the union step from a sample-dependent set of label representatives to deterministic-function probabilities stood out. A shortest-gap score was then designed to make every fixed threshold rarely exceptional while an empirically chosen threshold remains exceptional with nonvanishing probability.

**Verification method.** Read all 42 original pages and every appendix proof; rechecked original rendered PDF pages 5–6 and 21–23 against the construction, along with the relevant downstream assumptions and proofs. Verified each theorem assumption, the exact spacing/pair-area bound, the rank/CDF inconsistency argument, and the finite Lemma 9 contradiction. Executed the saved controls. A second auditor independently read the relevant original hypotheses/proof and rederived both probability arguments; their targeted note [unpublished artifact reference omitted] is saved. The author's 2010 thesis, PDF 183–184 and 198–200, repeats the same assumptions and union step without an additional restriction; this is corroboration, not the basis of the counterexample.

**Confidence: High.** The counterexample is analytic and satisfies all three printed conditions, including uniform fixed-function convergence at the required rate. It has positive cluster masses, label symmetry, measurable empirical minimizers, and no off-sample evaluations. Independent derivation and executable controls corroborate the argument. The scope is the general theorem; no unsupported failure of every particular NNC objective or historical experiment is inferred.

   ≤ (4n+2)[b_n + 2 exp(−2n ε²)] → 0.

sup_x |F_emp,n(x) − x| ≤ 0.05.

Q(f_n) − Q(f*) ≥ 0.25.

  ≤ s(F,2n) sup_f P(|Q_n(f) − Q'_n(f)| ≥ ε/2).

Read all 42 original pages and every appendix proof; rechecked original rendered PDF pages 5–6 and 21–23 against the construction, along with the relevant downstream assumptions and proofs. Verified each theorem assumption, the exact spacing/pair-area bound, the rank/CDF inconsistency argument, and the finite Lemma 9 contradiction. Executed the saved controls. A second auditor independently read the relevant original hypotheses/proof and rederived both probability arguments; their targeted note [unpublished artifact reference omitted] is saved. The author's 2010 thesis, PDF 183–184 and 198–200, repeats the same assumptions and union step without an additional restriction; this is corroboration, not the basis of the counterexample.

It has positive cluster masses, label symmetry, measurable empirical minimizers, and no off-sample evaluations. Independent derivation and executable controls corroborate the argument. The scope is the general theorem; no unsupported failure of every particular NNC objective or historical experiment is inferred.

findings.title: Tree-supported SOC constraints can jointly outperform LP-S
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2009__accepted__v10-kumar09a-01 — Tree-supported SOC constraints can jointly outperform LP-S
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Theorem 4, PDF page 24 / journal page 94; its reduction from multiple trees on PDF pages 22–23 / journal pages 92–93; the resulting all-tree feasibility claim on PDF page 28 / journal page 98. Definitions of the support graph are on PDF pages 19–21 / journal pages 89–91. The abstract and Section 2.1 advertise this generalization beyond LP-S versus SOCP-MS as a major result.

**Affected claim and assumptions.** Theorem 4 states that SOCP relaxations whose constraints are defined only using graphs that form trees are dominated by LP-S. The support graph G^k includes only original MRF edges with a nonzero entry in C^k; C^k may additionally contain coefficients on pairs that are not MRF edges, as explicitly illustrated by Equation (39). All constraints operate on the same matrix X. The paper expressly claims the result holds for overlapping trees, by splitting objective parameters. Its auxiliary assumptions allow the usual box and uniqueness constraints, diagonal X=1, symmetry and all SOCP-MS constraints. The example below satisfies these assumptions, uses nonnegative d and permits both signs of edge weights, as Theorem 4 does. It does not invoke Theorem 5's distinct same-sign-cycle hypothesis.

### Exact counterexample

Take four binary variables a,b,c,d on the cycle

\[
\mathcal E=\{(a,b),(b,c),(c,d),(a,d)\}.
\]

Use the selected label 0 and abbreviate its spin coordinates by a,b,c,d and pair entries by X_ab, etc. Introduce two PSD, rank-one constraint matrices on these four coordinates:

\[
C_1=v_1v_1^T,\quad v_1=(1,-2,1,0)^T,
\qquad
C_2=v_2v_2^T,\quad v_2=(1,0,-1,2)^T.
\]

All entries involving label 1 are zero. Their observed-edge supports are respectively the paths a–b–c and a–d–c, so each G^k is a tree under the paper's exact definition. They share only the auxiliary nonedge entry X_ac and the nodes a,c; their observed-edge sets are even disjoint. Include these two SOC constraints and all the standard SOCP-MS constraints. Since diagonal entries equal one, the additional constraints are

\[
(a-2b+c)^2\le 6-4X_{ab}-4X_{bc}+2X_{ac},
\]

\[
(a-c+2d)^2\le 6+4X_{ad}-4X_{cd}-2X_{ac}.
\]

The squared convention is derived explicitly in Section 1.5.1 and used in Equation (41). Equations (34)/(38) omit that superscript typographically. The counterexample also works under their literal unsquared reading: each left side is nonnegative, the attaining solution below has x=0, and every integral v_k^T x here is an even integer, so |v_k^T x|≤(v_k^T x)^2. Thus the ambiguity does not affect the gap or validity on integer labelings.

Adding them, with

\[
T=X_{ab}+X_{bc}+X_{cd}-X_{ad},
\]

gives the global certificate

\[
0\le(a-2b+c)^2+(a-c+2d)^2\le12-4T,
\qquad T\le3.
\]

The common objective can be chosen as

\[
E(x,X)=2-\frac{T}{2}.
\]

This is exactly a permitted unary/pairwise MRF objective, not an arbitrary extra criterion. For edges ab,bc,cd let s_e=1 and for ad let s_e=-1. Set the pairwise potential of label pair 00 to -2s_e and every other pairwise entry to zero. Set the label-0 unary potentials to (1/4,9/4,9/4,1/4), and all label-1 unary potentials to 1/4. Substitution into the paper's common relaxation objective and the binary uniqueness constraints cancels every linear spin term and yields E=2-T/2 exactly. These potentials factor as w_e d(i,j) with w_e=-s_e and d(i,j)=2 times the indicator of i=j=0, which is nonnegative. No semimetric or metric requirement is imposed in the general analysis; Section 1 explicitly allows arbitrary potentials. If representing edges in both orientations, halve each directed pair potential, leaving the same common objective.

LP-S permits x=0 and the locally consistent signed perfect correlations

\[
X_{ab}=X_{bc}=X_{cd}=1,\qquad X_{ad}=-1.
\]

For each edge e, fill its full 2×2 block by X_e;ij=s_e(-1)^{i+j}. These are valid uniform single-node marginals and matching pair marginals. Thus T=4 and E=0; box constraints also imply T≤4, proving the LP optimum is exactly zero.

In contrast, the summed SOC certificate proves E≥1/2 for every feasible solution of this allowed SOCP-T. This bound is attained: choose x=0, X_ac=0 and X_e;ij=(3/4)s_e(-1)^{i+j}. Set other cross-node nonedge entries to zero and within-node blocks to [[1,-1],[-1,1]]. Every box, symmetry, uniqueness, SOCP-MS and additional SOC constraint is satisfied. The point even satisfies edge marginalization, though SOCP-T does not require it. Both additional SOC inequalities are equalities. Consequently

\[
\min(\operatorname{LP-S})=0
\quad<\quad
\min(\operatorname{SOCP-T})=\frac12.
\]

This is the reverse of the advertised domination. All sixteen integer labelings remain feasible; their minimum energy is one, independently enumerated by the exact script. Hence this is a legitimate, strictly tighter convex relaxation, with finite nonnegative integer energies.

### Why the proof fails

For the LP optimum, the first tree requires X_ac≥1, while the second requires X_ac≤-1. Each individual tree can use an auxiliary completion, but the two completions cannot be the same global X. Splitting the energy parameter into theta_1+theta_2, as proposed on PDF pages 22–23, does not duplicate or decouple that shared feasibility variable. The minimization equality in Equations (41)–(42) and the subsequent treatment of nonedge entries as independent trivial choices discard this dependence. The construction directly targets the asserted extension to arbitrary sets of trees, not exactness on a single tree-structured MRF.

**Discovery method.** Traced the extension from one fixed tree to several trees and checked whether overlapping supports shared nonedge matrix entries. A four-cycle allows two path constraints to demand opposite completions of the same nonedge.

**Verification method.** Exact SymPy/Fraction certificate checks the PSD rank-one matrices, observed-edge tree supports, all LP and SOCP-MS constraints, the attained SOCP point, symbolic equality of the permitted MRF objective with 2-T/2 and all sixteen integer labelings. The summed inequality proves a global gap, so no numerical solver tolerance is involved. Original rendered PDF pages 19, 22–24 and 28 were inspected. Parent and Genton independently checked the original scope and exact construction; their reviews were targeted checks, not second full-paper reviews.

Reproduce with:

`python '[unpublished artifact reference omitted]`

Artifacts: exact checker [unpublished artifact reference omitted], exact results [unpublished artifact reference omitted].

**Reason for rejection.** The false result is the main extension from known pairwise relaxations to a large purportedly LP-dominated family, explicitly identified as one of the main results on PDF page 24 and used to motivate the paper's tree-versus-cycle distinction. It is not a normalization, endpoint or constant-factor defect: a valid member of the supposedly dominated family is strictly stronger than LP-S. Giving each tree its own auxiliary copy would change the relaxation being classified; restricting all constraints to one common tree or to suitably compatible private completions withdraws the advertised arbitrary-tree family. A replacement criterion and analysis are required. The separate LP-S-versus-SOCP-MS result, tight independent-rounding bound and proposed cycle/clique examples are not refuted by this counterexample, and no empirical score failure is alleged (the paper presents illustrative constructions, not a benchmark experiment).

**Confidence.** High. Exact rational and symbolic certificates prove both optimum values, all assumptions were checked in original renders, and two independent targeted reviews confirmed the construction and scope.

Independent verification artifacts: parent checker [unpublished artifact reference omitted], parent results [unpublished artifact reference omitted], Genton checker [unpublished artifact reference omitted], Genton results [unpublished artifact reference omitted]. Both independent reviews were targeted; the full-paper coverage and remaining screened claims are documented in review notes [unpublished artifact reference omitted].

findings.title: The multi-task updates are incompatible conditionals, so the claimed Dirichlet-process posterior does not exist
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2009__accepted__v10-li09b__I01 — The multi-task updates are incompatible conditionals, so the claimed Dirichlet-process posterior does not exist
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Section 5.3, Equation (57), PDF page 21 / journal page 1151, and Equations (58)–(60), PDF page 22 / journal page 1152; the exact Gibbs-posterior assertion in Section 5.4, PDF page 23; their use in Section 5.5 and Table 2, PDF pages 24 and 29–30. The contribution is advertised in the abstract, introduction PDF page 3, and conclusion PDF page 48.

**Affected claim and assumptions.** The paper claims to derive one Dirichlet-process posterior for the task clusters and their shared regionalized policies. Equation (57) is presented as an exact conditional posterior for a task's cluster indicator. Equation (58) is presented as the exact conditional posterior for the policy of a given cluster. Section 5.4 explicitly proposes Gibbs sampling by alternating these conditionals and says the stationary samples represent the posterior. Variational approximations are introduced later in Section 5.5.

Using a nonnegative value function in place of a likelihood is not itself the error: a normalized value times a prior is a coherent, nonstandard density, as explicitly defined in Equation (38). The error is that the two proposed multi-task conditionals cannot belong to any one joint distribution. The counterexample below uses the stated finite action/state model, a soft behavior policy, positive rewards, proper episodes, and the stated product-of-Dirichlets base.

**Reproducible example.** Take two tasks. In each, there is one nonterminal state and one observation. Either of two actions ends the episode in an absorbing state; all later rewards are zero. The RPR has one decision state, so its only nontrivial parameter is

\[
p=\pi(a),\qquad \pi(b)=1-p,\qquad 0<p<1.
\]

Let the behavior policy choose each action with probability \(1/2\), and collect two episodes per task, one using each action. Let the rewards for actions \((a,b)\) be \((2,1)\) in task 1 and \((1,2)\) in task 2. Both data sets are valid realizations of the soft behavior policy. Equation (11), including its importance weights, gives exactly

\[
V_1(p)=\tfrac12\{2p/(1/2)+(1-p)/(1/2)\}=1+p,
\]

\[
V_2(p)=\tfrac12\{p/(1/2)+2(1-p)/(1/2)\}=2-p.
\]

These also equal the actual expected task values. Thus this example introduces no sampling error into the value functions. Use DP precision \(\alpha=1\) and \(G_0=\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)\), the uniform Dirichlet base for the action probabilities. The one-dimensional initial-state and transition distributions are deterministic. The two tasks have equal episode counts, so replacing a sum by a weighted pooling average only multiplies it by a constant and cannot repair the discrepancy.

**The incompatible joined-policy distribution.** Write \(J\) for the partition in which both tasks share a policy, and \(S\) for the partition with separate policies. For a singleton cluster, Equation (38), or Equation (58) applied to one task, gives policy density proportional to \(G_0(p)V_m(p)\). The paper also expressly states that distinct cluster policies are conditionally independent given the partition (end of PDF page 22). Hence, on \(S\), the density of the two policies \((p,q)\) has shape

\[
s(p,q)=c\,V_1(p)V_2(q),\qquad c>0,
\]

where the common constant includes the probability of \(S\). Let \(j(q)\) denote the joint density of the shared policy and the event \(J\).

Given the other task's policy \(q\), Equation (57) assigns task 1 to that existing cluster with weight \(V_1(q)\), and to a new cluster with weight

\[
\alpha z_1,\qquad z_1=\int_0^1 V_1(p)\,dp=3/2.
\]

A newly created singleton policy has density \(V_1(p)/z_1\). Equivalently, the conditional ratio of the existing-cluster atom to the new-policy density at \(p\) is

\[
\frac{V_1(q)}{\alpha V_1(p)}.
\]

For any joint law having these conditionals, the same ratio is \(j(q)/s(p,q)\). Substituting the split density forces

\[
j(q)=\frac{c}{\alpha}V_1(q)V_2(q).
\]

Therefore the normalized shared-policy conditional must be

\[
 p(p\mid J,D_1,D_2)
 =\frac{(1+p)(2-p)}{\int_0^1(1+u)(2-u)\,du}
 =\frac6{13}(2+p-p^2).
\tag{*}
\]

By contrast, Equation (58) gives

\[
p_{\rm paper}(p\mid J,D_1,D_2)
=\frac{V_1(p)+V_2(p)}{\int_0^1[V_1(u)+V_2(u)]\,du}
=1.
\]

The two continuous densities disagree on open intervals, so versions of conditionals on null sets cannot resolve the contradiction. For example, their density ratios at \(p=1/2\) and \(p=1/4\) are respectively \(36/35\) and \(1\). Their second moments, which avoid any pointwise-density convention, are respectively \(43/130\) and \(1/3\).

The compatible alternative determined by Equation (57) is explicit: the DP prior multiplied by \(V_1(p_1)V_2(p_2)\). With \(\alpha=1\), its total normalizer is \(53/24\), its sharing probability is \(26/53\), and its joined-policy density is (*). It provides a control for all assignment and singleton updates, while refuting the proposed sum-based cluster update. This argument does not presuppose that the task values are ordinary likelihoods; it follows directly from the paper's own conditional ratios.

**Why the stated qualifications do not resolve it.** Equations (57) and (58) are derived in the same subsection as exact parts of one posterior, and Section 5.4 explicitly alternates them. They are not presented as two unrelated objectives or as already approximate conditionals. The variational approximation in Section 5.5 cannot approximate a joint posterior with incompatible exact conditionals. A Markov chain constructed by these updates may still have a stationary distribution, but its stationary law cannot have all the conditional distributions claimed here.

Changing Equation (58) to a product would make a coherent product-of-task-values pseudo-posterior, but it changes the paper's cluster-pooling objective and posterior distributions. The large-mixture structure in Equations (59)–(60), the motivation for the hybrid method in Section 5.4, and the single-pool variational update in Table 2 are derived specifically from the sum. They would need new multi-task derivations and changed updates. Alternatively, retaining the sum-based cluster objective requires different assignment conditionals; Equation (57) cannot be retained. Renaming the existing procedure as a heuristic abandons the advertised DP-posterior construction and posterior-inference interpretation. The change can alter the policy optimum: for valid one-step task values V1(p)=1+2p and V2(p)=2−p, the sum has its maximum at p=1 whereas the product has its maximum at p=3/4. These are substantive choices between different multi-task models, not a normalization constant or indexing correction.

**Discovery method.** Trace the task-assignment conditional and the shared-policy conditional back to the same proposed posterior. Reduce the RPR to a one-parameter terminating control problem, then compare the conditional ratio for joining a cluster with the density required by the cluster update.

**Verification method.** Read all 56 original pages, including appendices A–D; visually inspect the original Equations (38), (57), (58)–(60), the exact Gibbs assertion, and Table 2. Independently derive the normalized distributions using exact integration and verify them in `check.py` / `results.json`. The script also checks 150 separate normalized RPR latent-chain and corrected maximum-value EM controls, demonstrating that the posterior contradiction does not rely on rejecting the separate single-task construction. The root reviewer independently read original PDF pages 3, 9, 18, 21–23, and 29–31 and verified the exact integrals, normalized densities, density ratio, moment discrepancy, and importance-weighted value identities; see `root-targeted-check.py` and `root-targeted-results.json`. That second review was targeted, not a second full-paper audit. These are new analytical/computational checks, not authenticated historical experiment reruns.

**Reason for rejection.** Multi-task sharing through a derived DP posterior, together with its hybrid Gibbs-variational inference, is a central contribution identified in the title, abstract, introduction, technical development, and conclusion. The asserted posterior and inference interpretation fail in an elementary case inside the stated model, before any approximation or convergence issue. Restoring coherence requires choosing a different multi-task objective and changing the central posterior or allocation updates and their analysis. The single-task RPR representation, its properly indexed empirical-value EM update, the per-decision importance-sampling identity, and reported historical performance numbers are not refuted by this issue. No claim is made that a corrected method reverses any historical ranking.

findings.title: Marginal Gaussianization does not give the claimed model-free joint-oracle risk consistency
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2009__accepted__v10-liu09a-01 — Marginal Gaussianization does not give the claimed model-free joint-oracle risk consistency
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Theorem 8, PDF page 11, journal page 2305; the third inequality of the concluding risk chain in its proof, PDF page 32, journal page 2326. The model-free interpretation is explicit immediately above Theorem 8. Introduction PDF page 2 promises consistency in risk, model selection, and estimation; PDF pages 3–4 define persistency as approximation of the best model without assuming the true distribution lies in the fitted family.

**Affected claim and assumptions.** Theorem 8 states that the Winsorized estimator is persistent relative to every bounded monotone transformation and admissible precision matrix, even when the distribution is not nonparanormal. It assumes only the stated dimension and parameter-class restrictions for this conclusion. The estimator first fixes the marginal normal-score transformations, then minimizes the criterion over the precision matrix. The proof instead uses an empirical joint-minimization inequality over both transformations and precision matrices.

The following counterexample has fixed dimension, bounded continuous observations, and zero means and unit variances. Its competing transformations also preserve these moments. It therefore does not exploit arbitrary rescaling or a constant transformation. It works both for the printed inverse-norm constraint and after the natural correction to the precision-norm constraint used by the proof.

**Reproducible counterexample.** Let \(B\) be uniform on \(\{-1,1\}\), and let \(U_1,U_2\) be independent uniform random variables on \([1,2]\), independent of \(B\). Set

\[
 s=\sqrt{7/3},\qquad X_j=BU_j/s,\qquad j=1,2.
\]

This is a continuous distribution on two squares. Its marginal distributions are continuous. Directly,

\[
 E X_j=0,\quad E X_j^2=1,\quad
 \rho_X=E X_1X_2=\frac{(3/2)^2}{7/3}=\frac{27}{28}.
\]

Let \(g\) agree with the identity on \([-a,a]\), where \(a=2/s\), and extend it outside this interval by

\[
 g(x)=a+1-e^{-(x-a)}\quad (x>a),\qquad g(-x)=-g(x).
\]

It is bounded, continuously differentiable, and strictly increasing. It agrees with the identity on the entire support of each observation, so it preserves zero means and unit variances. For every fixed positive \(C\), it belongs to the theorem's \(\mathcal M_n\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). Its transformed covariance and optimal precision satisfy

\[
 \Sigma_X=\begin{pmatrix}1&27/28\\27/28&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \det\Sigma_X=\frac{55}{784},\qquad
 \Omega_X=\Sigma_X^{-1},\qquad \|\Omega_X\|_1=56.
\]

All displayed numerical norm sums here include every matrix entry. They therefore also upper-bound the off-diagonal sums used for the penalty on PDF page 8. This avoids relying on whether the theorem's norm notation retains that penalty convention or the proof's full-entry Hölder bound.

Now let \(h_j=\Phi^{-1}\circ F_j\), the population limit of the estimator. Given \(B\), its two coordinates are independent signed half-normal variables. Each marginal is standard normal, and

\[
 E(h_j\mid B)=B\sqrt{2/\pi},\qquad
 \rho_h=E h_1h_2=2/\pi.
\]

Consequently

\[
 \Sigma_h=\begin{pmatrix}1&2/\pi\\2/\pi&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \det\Sigma_h=1-4/\pi^2,\qquad
 \|\Sigma_h^{-1}\|_1=\frac{2\pi}{\pi-2}<6.
\]

Take \(p=2\), \(\xi=1/2\), and \(L_n=60\). Both precision matrices are strictly inside the corrected class with full-entry norm \(\|\Omega\|_1\le60\), and hence also inside its off-diagonal-norm version. They are also strictly inside the printed class \(\|\Omega^{-1}\|_1\le60\), because their covariance norms are \(55/14\) and \(2+4/\pi\), respectively. The dimension condition holds eventually, and the asserted error rate is \(60\sqrt{\log n}/n^{1/4}\to0\).

For completeness, the empirical transformation does converge to \(h\) in both test and sample second moments. Write \(\delta_n=1/(4n^{1/4}\sqrt{\pi\log n})\) and \(a_n=\sqrt{2\log n/n}\). The DKW event \(\|\widehat F_j-F_j\|_\infty\le a_n\) has probability tending to one, and \(a_n=o(\delta_n)\). On \(F_j(X_j)\in[2\delta_n,1-2\delta_n]\), the quantile derivative is at most \(\sqrt{2\pi}/\delta_n\), yielding a squared error \(O(a_n^2/\delta_n^2)=o(1)\). On the complementary tails, the clipped score is squared-bounded by \(2\log(1/\delta_n)\); their probability, and their empirical frequency on the DKW event, are \(O(\delta_n)\). The true normal-score tail second moment is \(O(\delta_n\log(1/\delta_n))\). Thus all these tail terms vanish; for sample true-score tails the same conclusion follows by Markov's inequality. Cauchy–Schwarz and the ordinary law of large numbers give both sample covariance and population second-moment convergence to \(\Sigma_h\). The raw sample mean and scale in Equation (7) converge to zero and one because the observations are bounded, so retaining those terms does not change the limit.

For sufficiently large samples, the unconstrained unique precision minimizer \(S_n(\widetilde f)^{-1}\) is feasible in either norm class. Therefore \(\widehat\Omega_n\to\Sigma_h^{-1}\). At a covariance-optimal precision, the risk defined in Theorem 8 is

\[
 R(f,\Sigma_f^{-1})=\frac12\{2+\log\det\Sigma_f-2\log(2\pi)\}
\]

for these zero-mean, two-dimensional transformations. Since the oracle class contains \((g,\Omega_X)\),

\[
 \begin{split}
 \liminf_{n\to\infty}\left[
 R(\widetilde f_n,\widehat\Omega_n)
 -\inf_{f,\Omega}R(f,\Omega)\right]
 &\ge \frac12\log\left(\frac{1-4/\pi^2}{55/784}\right)\\
 &=1.0687016508236418\ldots>0
 \end{split}
\]

in probability. This contradicts the claimed vanishing rate. The statement should be read as the corresponding probability lower bound (for every smaller positive constant); no almost-sure convergence is needed.

The printed inverse-norm class additionally permits a degenerate infinite oracle by taking a zero transformation and unbounded precision; controlling only off-diagonal precision entries has a similar diagonal issue. Those directly correctable class-definition problems are not the basis of this finding. Under the stronger repair that bounds the full-entry precision norm, the oracle is finite, yet the bounded, moment-normalized comparison above still has the same fixed positive gap.

**Error in the proof.** PDF page 32 asserts

\[
 \widehat R(\widetilde f_n,\widehat\Omega_n)
 \le \widehat R(f^*,\Omega^*).
\]

The estimator minimizes only over \(\Omega\), holding the normal-score \(\widetilde f_n\) fixed. It does not minimize over all monotone \(f\). Uniform convergence of empirical risks cannot supply this missing optimization property. The example shows that the property also fails in the population limit.

**Discovery method.** Trace the risk proof's final oracle comparison back to the two-step estimator on PDF page 8; then compare two moment-normalized transforms under a common latent sign to separate marginal Gaussianization from joint risk minimization.

**Verification method.** Inspect original rendered Theorem 8 and proof pages, derive both covariance matrices and risk values analytically, establish the estimator limit by DKW and tail control, and run `check.py`/`results.json` in this checks directory. The script uses exact rational raw covariance and 70-digit score/risk constants, then fresh samples up to one million observations and an independent 250,000-point validation set. It includes Equation (7)'s sample locations/scales. These controls are a new implementation of the stated estimator, not authenticated historical experiment reruns.

**Specific rejection consequence.** Risk consistency under misspecification is one of the three explicitly advertised theoretical guarantees, and Theorem 8 is its sole model-free joint-oracle result. The failure is a fixed positive gap even at dimension two; it is not a rate constant, norm-notation correction, finite initialization term, or growth restriction. Restricting the oracle to the already selected normal-score transform, or assuming the distribution is nonparanormal, withdraws the promised comparison with the best monotone transformed model under misspecification. Jointly optimizing the transformations would replace the central two-step algorithm and needs a new analysis; PDF page 8 itself explains that such joint fitting is generally nonconvex. This finding does not refute the separate correctly specified covariance/graph-consistency results or the historical experiment scores.

**Confidence.** High. The fixed positive gap is analytic and respects both norm-class interpretations, continuous data, and the paper's moment-identifiability convention. All 34 pages, including the full Section 7 proofs and all figures/tables, were reviewed. Separate screened defects and the limits of historical replication are recorded in the full review notes.

**Independent verification and preserved evidence.** Parent and Genton independently inspected targeted original pages, checked the assumptions and rederived the covariance/risk calculations. These were targeted checks, not second full-paper reviews. Their independent calculations confirm the same positive gap and norm feasibility. **Location and claim.** Theorem 5(2), PDF page 8/printed 1518, asserts that when both graphs include the data-generating distribution, the log score ratio favoring the smaller graph is half the dimension difference times log n, with an O(log log n) almost-sure remainder. No full-support or strictly interior true-parameter assumption is imposed.

\[
P(X=1)=P(X=2)=\tfrac12,\qquad
P(Y=1)=\tfrac{99}{100},\quad P(Y=2)=\tfrac1{100},\qquad Z=X.
\]

The only boundary parameters are the deterministic conditional probabilities for Z. The smaller graph is parameter optimal; a graph of dimension 3 would be empty and could not represent X=Z. It is also faithful under the usual disjoint conditional-independence convention: Y is independent of (X,Z), while X and Z remain dependent with or without conditioning on Y. Exact rational checks of all nontrivial three-variable set-independence queries are saved in `faithfulness-checks.json`.

Use the same standard prior specification, BDeu with equivalent sample size 2, in both models. Each root has Beta(1,1) prior. A child with q binary-parent configurations has an independent Beta(1/q,1/q) prior in every row. Thus Z's two rows in `m_s` have Beta(1/2,1/2) priors, and its four rows in `m_l` have Beta(1/4,1/4) priors. All shapes are strictly positive; these are proper independent Beta priors allowed by the theorem. Choose equal positive graph priors if comparing graph posteriors. The theorem itself concerns the marginal scores, so no graph-prior adjustment is required.

\[
g_a(t)=\frac{\operatorname{Beta}(t+a,a)}{\operatorname{Beta}(a,a)}
=\frac{\Gamma(2a)}{\Gamma(a)}\frac{\Gamma(t+a)}{\Gamma(t+2a)}
\sim \frac{\Gamma(2a)}{\Gamma(a)}t^{-a}.
\]

\frac{\operatorname{score}_B(D_n\mid m_s)}{\operatorname{score}_B(D_n\mid m_l)}
=\frac{\prod_{x=1}^2 g_{1/2}(N_x)}{\prod_{x,y=1}^2 g_{1/4}(N_{xy})}.

\[
\frac{\operatorname{score}_B(D_n\mid m_s)}{\operatorname{score}_B(D_n\mid m_l)}
\longrightarrow
L=\frac{\Gamma(1/4)^4}{\pi^3}\sqrt{\frac{99}{100}\frac1{100}}
=0.554488162945929269\ldots<1
\quad\text{almost surely}.

| 20,000,000 | 0.5544877990 |

findings.title: The new conditional sign guarantees permit collider selection that reverses their conclusion
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2009__accepted__v10-vanderweele09a-01 — The new conditional sign guarantees permit collider selection that reverses their conclusion
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Propositions 7 and 8, PDF page 8 / journal page 706; their proofs in Appendix A.10–A.11, PDF pages 15–17 / journal pages 713–715. The common-cause definition is on PDF page 2 / journal page 700. The preceding paragraph on PDF page 7 and discussion on PDF page 8 expressly identify these conditional expectation results as new generalizations beyond earlier monotonicity results.

**Claim and assumptions.** Proposition 7 says that $E[Y\mid A,Q]$ is non-decreasing in binary $A$ if $A$ is not a descendant of $Y$, $Q$ consists of nondescendants of $A$ and $Y$, all directed $A$-to-$Y$ paths are positive, and every common cause in $C$ has equally signed directed paths to $A$ avoiding $Q$ and to $Y$ avoiding $\{Q,A\}$. Proposition 8 gives the reverse conditional expectation conclusion, $E[A\mid Y,Q]$ non-decreasing in binary $Y$, under the same graph conditions. These conditions do not prevent $Q$ from opening a collider path.

**Counterexample.** Use five binary variables with DAG

$$
C_1\to A\to Y,\qquad
C_1\to Q\leftarrow C_2\to Y,\qquad
C_1\to Y,\quad Q\to Y.
$$

Let $C_1,C_2$ be independent Bernoulli$(1/2)$ variables. Give every remaining node its own independent uniform error and let it be one when that error is at most the following conditional probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(A=1\mid C_1)&=\tfrac1{10}+\tfrac45C_1,\\
P(Q=1\mid C_1,C_2)&=\tfrac1{10}+\tfrac45\max(C_1,C_2),\\
P(Y=1\mid A,C_1,C_2,Q)&=\tfrac1{10}+\tfrac1{10}A+
\tfrac35C_2+\tfrac1{20}Q+\tfrac1{100}C_1.
\end{aligned}
$$

These equations satisfy the paper's independent-error causal model. Every edge has a positive monotonic structural effect under its stronger Definition 1, hence also a weak positive monotonic effect. All 32 joint cells have positive probability; the minimum is $11/40000$. There is no zero-support or conditioning-version ambiguity.

$Q$ is a nondescendant of both $A$ and $Y$ and is also a parent/ancestor of $Y$. The only directed path from $A$ to $Y$ is its positive direct edge. The common-cause set, under the paper's definition requiring a route to $Y$ not through $A$, is exactly $C=\{C_1\}$. The path $C_1\to A$ is positive, and the path $C_1\to Y$ avoiding both $Q$ and $A$ is positive. Thus the common-cause condition is nonvacuous and every stated assumption holds.

Nevertheless, in stratum $Q=1$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[C_2\mid A=0,Q=1]&=\tfrac56,&
E[C_2\mid A=1,Q=1]&=\tfrac{45}{86},\\
E[C_1\mid A=0,Q=1]&=\tfrac16,&
E[C_1\mid A=1,Q=1]&=\tfrac{81}{86}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently,

$$
E[Y\mid A=0,Q=1]=\tfrac{391}{600},\qquad
E[Y\mid A=1,Q=1]=\tfrac{4931}{8600},
$$

and

$$
E[Y\mid A=1,Q=1]-E[Y\mid A=0,Q=1]
=-\tfrac{101}{1290}<0.
$$

This directly contradicts Proposition 7. Exact enumeration also gives

$$
E[A\mid Y=0,Q=1]=\tfrac{1223}{1850},\qquad
E[A\mid Y=1,Q=1]=\tfrac{4931}{8450},
$$

whose difference is $-2424/31265<0$, contradicting Proposition 8. Both contradictions arise from the same omitted selection-path condition, so they are one issue.

**Failed proof step.** Appendix A.10 claims that $E[Y\mid A,Q,C]$ is non-decreasing in each common-cause coordinate by applying Proposition 4. Here, for every fixed $a$,

$$
E[Y\mid A=a,Q=1,C_1=0]=\tfrac{69}{100}+\tfrac a{10},\qquad
E[Y\mid A=a,Q=1,C_1=1]=\tfrac{46}{100}+\tfrac a{10}.
$$

It instead decreases in $C_1$. The proposed application of Proposition 4 fails its backdoor-blocking requirements: conditioning on $Q$ opens $C_1\to Q\leftarrow C_2\to Y$. In the graph used above, conditioning on $A$ and the supposed earlier variables does not block the backdoor $Q\leftarrow C_2\to Y$ required by that invocation. Appendix A.11 relies on the same incorrect conditional-monotonicity claim. The common-cause definition refers to directed causal paths and does not include this opened selection path.

**Discovery method.** Traced the conditional-expectation proof back to Proposition 4's precise blocking assumptions, then constructed a collider stratum that is permitted by the new Propositions 7–8. Added positive direct effects and positive noise to eliminate vacuous paths, an empty common-cause set, nonancestral conditioning and support degeneracy as possible explanations.

**Verification method.** The executable `check.py` enumerates all 32 cells using exact rational arithmetic, verifies support and graph conditions, computes both reversed conditional differences and the failed proof step, and includes a simpler corroborating witness. It also checks 3,074 conditional cells plus 584 nonempty-mediator cells satisfying Proposition 4's actual backdoor criteria and independently reproduces both Appendix B counterexamples. Root separately read the original definitions/statements/proofs, inspected the critical original renders and independently enumerated both witnesses; its artifacts confirm the exact constants without importing the candidate formulas.

Evidence is in `[unpublished artifact reference omitted]`:

- Exact executable check [unpublished artifact reference omitted] and results [unpublished artifact reference omitted].
- Independent stronger-witness check [unpublished artifact reference omitted] and independent simpler-witness check [unpublished artifact reference omitted].
- Original propositions [unpublished artifact reference omitted] and Appendix A.10 [unpublished artifact reference omitted].

Reproduce with `python check.py` from the evidence directory.

**Reason for rejection.** This theoretical paper expressly advances Propositions 7–8 as new conditional sign constraints beyond previous results. They infer a positive association from the allowed signed graph even though a strictly positive, fully monotone causal model produces a negative association. This invalidates that advertised generalization and its proof, rather than merely weakening a constant or repairing a test's direction. Requiring safe conditioning sets would exclude the demonstrated allowed structures and needs a new selection-aware graphical condition/proof; restricting $Q$ to ancestors, requiring nonempty common causes, or strengthening weak monotonicity does not repair it. Reverting to Proposition 4's backdoor-blocking regime withdraws the claimed relaxation. Other results, including the backdoor-conditioned statements, unconditional binary implications and the specific motivating graph's properly directed test, are not claimed refuted by this issue.

**Confidence: High.** Exact full-support arithmetic, explicit monotonic independent-error structural equations, original-render assumption checks and separate parent enumeration agree. The finding concerns the paper's formal scope, not a medical empirical claim or an undocumented historical implementation.

findings.title: The correctness proof assumes a DAG-compatible intermediate pattern where the prescribed collider constraints are incompatible
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2009__accepted__v10-yehezkel09a-01 — The correctness proof assumes a DAG-compatible intermediate pattern where the prescribed collider constraints are incompatible
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF 7, printed page 1533, orientation and partial-topological-order description; Figure 4, PDF 9, printed page 1535, steps A2/B2 and the ancestor/descendant decomposition; Proposition 2 and its proof, PDF 16–18, printed pages 1542–1544. The worked example on PDF 12 uses exogenous incoming edges as orientation context. The argument is central to the claimed correctness and efficient autonomous recursion.

**Affected claim and assumptions.** Proposition 2 promises the correct pattern for a faithful DAG of any d-separation resolution. Its induction assumes that orientation and decomposition preserve the parent candidates needed for subsequent separating sets. The proof applies an induction hypothesis about complete true graphs of resolution (m) to an intermediate skeleton obtained by testing only through order (m) in a higher-resolution graph, then invokes anytime-FCI soundness. Such an intermediate skeleton need not support an ordinary DAG-compatible partially directed graph. Anytime FCI uses partial ancestral endpoint information; its result does not supply the missing rule for discarding conflicting collider heads, treating the remaining arrows as parent/topological information, and preserving autonomy.

The example below has only six binary observed variables, maximum fan-in 2, d-separation resolution 1, strictly positive cell probabilities, faithfulness and exact CI decisions. It does not depend on sampling error or large degree.

**Exact incompatible intermediate requirements.** Take

$$
1\longrightarrow4\longleftarrow3\longrightarrow6\longleftarrow5,
\qquad6\longrightarrow2.
$$

After completing every order-0 CI test, the skeleton has edges

$$
14,\;23,\;24,\;25,\;26,\;34,\;36,\;46,\;56.
$$

Every absent pair has the empty separating set. The paper's unshielded-triplet instruction therefore requires, among others,

$$
1\to4\leftarrow2
\quad\text{and}\quad
4\to2\leftarrow5.
$$

The first requires (2\to4), while the second requires (4\to2). Likewise, (1\to4\leftarrow6) and (4\to6\leftarrow5) require both heads on (4-6). No processing order can simultaneously satisfy these instructions with an ordinary acyclic directed/undirected PDAG. Choosing an order merely chooses which required head to ignore. The paper supplies no conflict policy or invariant proving that discarding heads preserves its subsequent ancestry/autonomy claims.

This is a concrete failure of the proof's necessary intermediate-state premise. The true graph has resolution 1, but its completed order-0 information is not the DAG-compatible resolution-0 pattern assumed by the induction. The four-node argument in Section 3.2.2, about retaining a valid arm when another arm is removed, does not address this incompatibility.

**A strictly positive faithful distribution.** Let (X_1,X_3,X_5) be independent binary roots with success probabilities (41/100,53/100,47/100). Specify:

| Variable | Parent assignments | Conditional probability of value 1 |
|---|---|---|
| (X_4) | ((X_1,X_3)=00,01,10,11) | (11/100,37/100,61/100,83/100) |
| (X_6) | ((X_3,X_5)=00,01,10,11) | (13/100,31/100,67/100,89/100) |
| (X_2) | (X_6=0,1) | (17/100,79/100) |

All 64 joint cells are positive, with minimum (324674449/10^{12}). Exact rational enumeration checks every one of the 240 pair/conditioning-subset CI queries, in every conditioning stratum, against graphical d-separation. They all agree. The maximum minimum separator size is 1. Independently enumerating the 32 orientations of the true five-edge skeleton leaves exactly one acyclic graph with its unshielded colliders, so the correct CPDAG is the displayed DAG.

**Conditional wrong-output corroboration.** The archived author routines reset an edge with two inferred heads to undirected. This policy is present in the source, rather than specified in the paper. Applying that policy and ordinary, correctly implemented Meek propagation after the complete marginal pass leaves initial arrows

$$
1\to4,\;3\to4,\;3\to6,\;5\to6,\;3\to2,\;5\to2
$$

and undirected edges (2-4,4-6,2-6). In the source's column order:

1. (5\to2-4), with 5 and 4 nonadjacent, makes rule 1 direct (2\to4).
2. (1\to4-6), with 1 and 6 nonadjacent, makes rule 1 direct (4\to6).
3. The path (2\to4\to6) makes rule 2 direct (2\to6), reversing the true edge (6\to2).

This output is acyclic, and every remaining unshielded collider belongs to the initial CI-declared collider set. Thus the paper's prohibition of new colliders, interpreted relative to that initial set, does not exclude this trace. On all 720 relabelings, the same ordinary propagation order reverses a true edge in 120 cases. This is not a claim that every order or every unprinted conflict policy gives the same wrong output.

The resulting split treats node 6 as a descendant outside the ancestor subproblem containing node 2. False edges (3\to2) and (5\to2) then survive: their unique true open paths are (3\to6\to2) and (5\to6\to2), so a separating set must include 6. But 6 is outside that subproblem and excluded as a directed child of 2. The complete native controlled trace confirms the two surviving false edges and the reversed true edge. Additional data or recursion orders cannot supply a node excluded by this split.

**Repair checks and precise limits.** This finding does not claim a false final output under every possible completion of the underspecified orientation operation. A stricter interpretation forbids restoring even collider triples erased by the two-head reset. An explicit post-reset no-new-collider/no-cycle guard, together with deferring A2 until B2, passes 400 fresh six-node and 400 seven-node controls. Those successes are retained. They are not a proof that this different conflict/orientation policy preserves all true parents and autonomy at every order. A short root-ancestor-set argument explains its safety at completed order 0; it does not provide the missing higher-order invariant.

Simpler repairs were tested first. Correcting the source's R3 test and numeric representation is insufficient. Completing its collider scan still leaves 510 failures across all 8,782 five-node equivalence classes. Deferring A2 fixes those five-node cases but leaves the six-node failure above and other six/seven-node failures. Thus the essential proof gap is not resolved by the isolated source typo, missed collider arm or one-pass scheduling change.

The untouched archived prototype itself returns the correct graph on this particular six-node fixture, because its logical working matrix suppresses the stated early Meek propagation; it has different exact orientation failures. No modified implementation is presented as the historical program. Its supplied 2011 Alarm demonstration was reproduced exactly, including SHD 2 and CI counts. The 2009 empirical tables, historical prediction rankings and every possible conservative repair are not alleged false.

**Reason for rejection.** Formal correctness of the new recursive learner is a main contribution. Its efficiency mechanism uses early directions to exclude parent candidates and split the graph; the required safety premise fails on a small, positive, faithful input in the intended domain. The proof does not define or justify a safe treatment of the resulting conflicting heads, and the anytime-PAG analogy does not establish ordinary-PDAG autonomy. Accepting the guarantee requires a specified revised orientation policy and an all-orders proof that it preserves true parents and eventual complete patterns. Passing modified finite controls cannot replace that missing central argument. This is distinct from the routine complexity/source corrections screened elsewhere in the review.

**Discovery method.** Traced the induction, early-orientation rules and anytime-FCI transfer; recovered the author implementation; compared native oracle results with independently enumerated CPDAGs; tested simple repairs before isolating the incompatible completed-order constraints.

**Verification method.** A separately written exact-rational Python certificate imports no author routines. It checks positivity, all 240 CI queries, resolution, the unique true MEC, conflicting requirements, the conditional Meek trace, acyclicity, initial-versus-final collider sets, and all 720 relabelings. A native controlled full-recursion trace corroborates the conditional exclusion failure. A second auditor independently checked all 240 CI queries and conflicting requirements with a separate ancestral-moral d-separation oracle, and inspected the cited original pages. That was a targeted check, not a second full-paper review.

**Confidence.** High in the incompatible prescribed constraints and invalid intermediate-state proof premise. The wrong-output trace is explicitly conditional on the documented source reset and ordinary propagation; no unconditional counterexample to every unspecified resolver is claimed.
